newsitem.title: USA: US FCC oks rules to cut costs of overseas calls.
newsitem.headline: US FCC oks rules to cut costs of overseas calls.

text.p: Federal regulators on Thursday approved rules to slash the price of overseas phone calls in a move aimed at saving American consumers and businesses billions of dollars a year.

Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt predicted his agency's action will cut the average price of an international call from the United States to 20 cents a minute from the current 88 cents within five years.

The FCC order, which takes effect at the start of next year and will be phased in over five years, set "benchmark" rates to push down the so-called "settlement" rates that U.S. phone companies pay overseas carriers to complete U.S.-originated calls.

The benchmark targets -- which range from 15 cents a minute to 23 cents a minute -- are sharply below the level that many overseas state-run phone monopolies charge to complete calls. The benchmarks will vary depending on a foreign country's income level. The FCC said the 88 cents a minute that U.S. consumers now pay for an international call is more than six times the cost of the average domestic long-distance call, even though the costs of the calls are not much different.

"Our benchmarks will lead to much lower settlement rates, and thereby promote competition and lower costs for consumers," Peter Cowhey, head of the FCC's international bureau, said at a public meeting where the rules were adopted.

U.S. carriers in 1996 paid about $5.4 billion more than foreign carriers paid their U.S. counterparts to complete calls. That deficit has nearly doubled since 1990, reflecting in part the inflated costs charged by overseas carriers as well as the large immigrant population in the United States that makes overseas calls, FCC officials said.
